content:
{'index': 0, 'translation': 'Last time I mentioned King Sir\'s 1987 translated and directed production of "Cyrano," where the gifted and proud big-nosed lover Cyrano felt cowardly and inferior before his beloved cousin Roxane. When I interviewed James Wong in 2015, I asked him:'}

{'index': 1, 'translation': '"Actually, would a man\'s talent make him feel inferior because of a big nose?"'}

{'index': 2, 'translation': '"He would when love comes; not usually, but once love arrives, he becomes a fragile little boy. Love is very幼稚." (audio)'}

{'index': 3, 'translation': "Precisely because his nose was different from others, Cyrano felt inferior. Love sometimes makes one so fragile, accepting only people's strengths and never their weaknesses—this is human nature, and it is also drama. Life and drama both need sublimation. James Wong said this was the last Romanticist play in France. An ugly man helping a handsome one write love letters to the woman he loves—just like many things in the world, appearance and truth are forever intertwined; utterly false yet not without sincerity. What a woman loves is the soul poured between the lines, to the point of madness."}

{'index': 4, 'translation': 'James Wong explained the backstory: "After Cyrano was ambushed and injured in the head, he still went to visit his cousin every week. His cousin didn\'t know he loved her deeply. He wrote letters on behalf of that handsome man to pursue his cousin. Just as that handsome man wanted to confess that the letters weren\'t written by him—because the woman said she loved his talent—at the moment of his confession, Christian was killed in battle. The cousin then took the letters and entered a convent. Cyrano went to visit her every week, telling her the news, chatting about idle things to make her happy. When he—"'}

{'index': 5, 'translation': 'Are half of the most beautiful stories in life lies?'}

{'index': 6, 'translation': 'The handsome Christian tried on the battlefield to pick up his pen and clarify the truth, but was immediately shot dead; his fresh blood stained the letter red; the tears on the letter were Cyrano\'s. Blood and tears are both real; their coexistence does not mean they came from the same man. The good and bad in life—if you are unwilling to bear them together, in the end, you may lose them all. "Everyone has their own wounds"—when I saw the final scene of the original, Cyrano, ambushed in the head and seriously wounded, came to the convent to find his cousin Roxane. Roxane noticed he was injured, and Cyrano told her a lie, saying—'}

{'index': 7, 'translation': 'He took from his embrace that love letter stained with fresh blood and tears—the one Roxane had always thought Christian wrote to her. She agreed to let Cyrano read it aloud. Here, Cyrano held the letter and began to read: "Farewell, Roxane, I am dying. The love I never spoke of weighs heavily on my heart. My eyes can no longer greedily gaze upon your every movement. When I think of you speaking, your fingers gently brushing your cheek—that gesture, is so unbearably familiar to me. Deep in my heart I am crying out: farewell!"'}

{'index': 8, 'translation': '"You read this letter so well, just as if…" Roxane.'}

{'index': 9, 'translation': '"My life, my love, my treasure, my beloved—my heart has always been buried between every beat of yours."'}

{'index': 10, 'translation': 'Inside the convent the light was dim; Cyrano could not possibly see the contents of the letter—this is the flaw in the drama. Yet, his familiar voice reading the love letter made Roxane recognise the sound of the soul she had always loved:'}

{'index': 11, 'translation': '"That person was actually you!"'}

{'index': 12, 'translation': '"No, Roxane, no!"'}

{'index': 13, 'translation': '"Every time you called my name, I should have known."'}

{'index': 14, 'translation': '"No, that wasn\'t me!" "That was you!" "I swear!"'}

{'index': 15, 'translation': '"Now I finally see through this generous lie—the love letters were actually written by you!"'}

{'index': 16, 'translation': '"No!"'}

{'index': 17, 'translation': '"Those sweet words, that mad love. It was all you!"'}

{'index': 18, 'translation': '"No!"'}

{'index': 19, 'translation': '"What moved me in the darkness was that voice!"'}

{'index': 20, 'translation': '"I swear, you have the wrong person!"'}

{'index': 21, 'translation': '"That soul—it is yours!"'}

{'index': 22, 'translation': '"I have never loved you!" "You loved me!"'}

{'index': 23, 'translation': '"No, that was him!"'}

{'index': 24, 'translation': '"You loved me!"'}

{'index': 25, 'translation': '"No!" (His voice grew weaker and weaker)'}

{'index': 26, 'translation': '"Your voice is trembling; your denials grow weaker and weaker!"'}

{'index': 27, 'translation': 'Drama is loving someone, words stuck in the throat, leaving only a "no"—the more one says it, the weaker and more panicked one becomes inside. Drama is loving someone, unable to confess, a whole life\'s fate twisted and rewritten by it. Drama is loving someone, knowing one cannot make them stay, yet through words and soul finding a path of deep affection. Drama is grappling all one\'s life with light and shadow, sorrow and joy, falsehood and truth. When Roxane discovered the true author of the love letters was the dying Cyrano, she said: "I loved a man, yet lost him twice."'}

{'index': 28, 'translation': 'Life slips away quietly, unnoticed and uncontrolled. Two men who loved her—in the end neither could have her—this is drama. She truly loved a soul, yet lost him twice: the first when Christian was killed in battle; the second when, just as she discovered Cyrano was the true author of the love letters, Cyrano died in her arms. The dialogue is like poetry—that too is drama.'}

{'index': 29, 'translation': '"The last few lines are also wonderful. As I pass through God\'s threshold, I will sweep away all the stars on the lintel; the only one flawless is the proud white plume on my head. So majestic." (James Wong audio)'}

{'index': 30, 'translation': 'A lifetime of牵挂—the world of drama'}

{'index': 31, 'translation': 'That year, watching King Sir\'s "Cyrano" in its final scene, in the pitch-black theatre, I sat in the middle front row, as if I alone were witnessing the end of the world, letting tears run wild, my heart churning. Returning to my own heart, what life ultimately needs, and what it possesses day after day, are forever separated by ten thousand mountains. "Cyrano" uses humour to convey the essence of tragedy: rare and precious. A lifetime of牵挂, a lifetime of searching—that is life. Thought is free. Apart from being moved and touched, I also realised for myself that a single drama class is enough to change—'}

{'index': 32, 'translation': 'What is a theatre? At that moment, the theatre was a place where, in the darkness, I could look ahead to the future. One need not become an actor, but must earnestly pursue the highest good and beauty. Missing out on the Academy, losing something, is in fact walking toward another possibility. What matters most is that you still know what it is you wish to pursue.'}

{'index': 33, 'translation': 'King Sir\'s stage productions opened my eyes. One of his early works at the Academy, "Under the Banyan Tree," was likewise a brilliant original play full of Hong Kong\'s local colour. In junior secondary I had heard of his productions of "The Horse," "The Death of Mozart," "Death of a Salesman" and "West Side Story"—I never had the chance to see any of them. What is even more regrettable is that I never had the opportunity to sit down with King Sir for a long talk about drama and life. Over a decade ago, through the late Lai Ming-fai, news officer at the Polytechnic University, I once stood by the side and observed King Sir in Hong Kong—'}

{'index': 34, 'translation': '"Whether with peers or with young people, he was always humble and polite, with a smile on his face. That was not acting, but a gentleman\'s cultivation from the heart, making one feel respected yet at ease."'}

{'index': 35, 'translation': 'In the 2018 citation when Hong Kong Shue Yan University conferred an honorary doctorate on Mr King Sir, I felt a particular kinship with the passage above. To take my own brief encounter with King Sir, his smile and the way he looked at you made you feel deeply respected and warmed the heart. I personally suspect his refusal to be interviewed was related to the tense relationship between the television station and the newspaper I worked for at the time.'}

{'index': 36, 'translation': 'Back then, when I wanted to enrol in the Academy, people all assumed I dreamed of becoming an actor, of going into performance. I immediately replied: "No, I want to study drama." That might be the world of directing, screenwriting, or literature. From junior secondary on, I had written two or three plays of my own, self-written, self-directed, self-acted, but that flame eventually died out, quietly buried in the depths of my heart—at one time it was a lingering regret.'}

{'index': 37, 'translation': 'Four years ago, when writing about Dickens for my Patreon, I read several related academic articles and only then understood how Dickens transformed from missing the chance to be an actor and a reporter into a literary giant of his generation. I gained a new perspective on the dream I had long cherished.'}

{'index': 38, 'translation': 'In his later years, Dickens personally performed readings of his own works—self-written, self-directed live readings—and the ticket revenue exceeded that of his novels, with more than half of his wealth coming from this (see the first Patreon article). He sublimated the passion for performance of his youth into the opportunity to read his own works aloud. The wonder of life lies not in merely realising a dream, but in transformation and sublimation. The greatest lesson in life that drama teaches is called "a blessing in disguise." Sometimes love cannot be attained, but if one makes good use of what one has in hand, amidst countless transformations—'}

{'index': 39, 'translation': "Last year in England, I walked past Dickens's old residence in Rochester. It is said that Dickens's father once encouraged his son to work hard, so that one day he could buy a house like that. Dickens eventually did buy this house, and it has been preserved to this day, together with a secondary school attached to it—the students there are truly fortunate."}

{'index': 40, 'translation': 'Life is like a play; there is no need to sigh over its twists and turns, for there may simply be too much worth appreciating. Once I understood this point, I poured my passion into free self-expression, becoming a journalist who loves to write about people. I pour my most intense feelings into true stories—stories that contain you, me and him—play after play of "word-made stagecraft." If they can move people\'s hearts, that is the warmest applause.'}

{'index': 41, 'translation': 'The pioneering and golden years of the Academy—the Hong Kong Academy for Performing Arts has been established for over forty years. At its founding, there were only four schools: Drama, Music, Dance, and Stage Technology (Technical Arts). Later, Film & Television and Cantonese Opera were added, making six in total. Looking back at this Academy I once failed to enter, in the mid-eighties no university campus could be so grand and elegant, with air-conditioning on all day. To preserve the venue and equipment, every corner was kept refreshingly cool. The brand-new carpet alternated between deep green and light green.'}

{'index': 42, 'translation': 'In the first few years after the Academy was founded, for various reasons, I often wandered through countless corners of this "large amusement park." Honestly, when I first walked in, I felt tiny and out of place—not because the place was vast, but because that atmosphere was so far from our daily life, yet open to everyone. Students from different backgrounds and classes came together to learn, bound by shared interests and ideals. It was a very special, yet not unbearably difficult, way of being.'}

{'index': 43, 'translation': "Whether King King-fai is a master depends on whether we have inherited an environment that nurtures masters. The Academy has developed for forty-two years; Hong Kong has established a set of systems and standards for the performing arts. The culture of drama, apart from blossoming and bearing fruit through different theatre companies, has also taken root and grown in the freedom of the Academy. King King-fai is a landmark of foundation-building. From his era onward, many professional theatre practitioners dedicated to drama education, together with their students, generation after generation—both able to perform and to teach—Hong Kong's."}
